title: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
snippet: Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access. more…
fullText:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

	

	

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.  

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

title: Maximizing Privacy? New Apple Home Security Cameras Reportedly Won’t Record Video
snippet: Instead of a watchable video stream, you’ll get text descriptions or alerts about detected people, pets or activity.
fullText:
From Flock AI-powered security cameras to Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, people are getting frustrated with their everyday movements being recorded and tracked. Apple likely smells a market opportunity to do something different.

According to Bloomberg News Managing Editor and Apple insider Mark Gurman, the company is developing a home security camera that can detect and notify about intruders — without capturing video footage. The device would be a companion to the new AI-powered home hub the company is slated to launch Oct. 13.

A representative for Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

			

More from CNET

Speaking on his brand-new Power On podcast, Gurman said the cameras would be smallish cylinders — “like a metal ChapStick” — and could be placed anywhere and everywhere in the home. Acting more like sensors than video recorders, the cameras would reportedly use AI facial recognition to determine who and what is moving around inside and outside the house. The devices have a low frame rate, which means they’ll take far fewer still images than typical video cameras.

The upcoming Apple home hub will also use facial and voice recognition to identify homeowners and other users, so the security cameras may work with that data.

The camera would use text descriptions to inform homeowners about what is happening, such as “the dog is in the kitchen” or “someone is outside the back door,” for example. Visual input would interpret an event, but no video footage would be captured, Gurman said on the podcast. “It’s analyzing your environment and your home and around your home, simply using AI. It’s a very similar technology that they’re using for the AirPods with cameras.”

Without stored footage of a burglary or other crimes in the home, however, it’s unclear how police would retrieve much identifying information in an investigation, Gurman said. “You need the actual tape. So, it will be interesting to see how Apple markets this.”

Assuaging surveillance fears

Gurman said that avoiding video recording could be a selling point for Apple amid growing backlash over the surveillance environment of Flock cameras, smart devices and personal tech, like AI-powered glasses.

Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses have acquired the nickname “pervert glasses” because some people are using them to secretly record mostly women without their knowledge. Meta is now reportedly developing glasses that don’t have cameras and will instead rely solely on AI for speech and listening.

Having a smart home device that doesn’t rely on recorded, stored and analyzed data is a good privacy element, says CNET home security expert Tyler Lacoma. Presumably, Apple would rely on some type of on-device feature for capturing data, but we don’t have details. Short-lived machine analysis is quite different from a watchable video stream. 

Gurman didn’t say what kind of technology would be used in the cameras, but noted that the new home hub would not use Face ID, which is used to unlock iPhones and iPads. Whatever biometric template is used in the home hub might be the same as the one used by the cameras.

Nonetheless, if Apple does rely on true facial recognition technology, that could “open up a big can of worms,” Lacoma said, pointing to lawsuits against smart home security companies Nest and Ring over their use of identity tracking.

Gurman dismissed the notion that Apple would violate its customers’ privacy, though he said he thought the company will still be accused of turning over personal data to government agencies.

“Anyone who covers Apple close enough, or even remotely close enough, would know that would be hogwash for Apple,” Gurman said. “But I think we all know the reality is far different that Apple won’t be doing that with our data.”

Since Apple hasn’t publicly released the product yet, we’ll have to wait and see.

title: Instinct brings its AI agent to group chats, even for friends without an account
snippet: Instinct is launching group chats that let friends use its AI agent together for tasks like planning trips, organizing carpools, and coordinating events. The company says personal accounts remain separate, with permission required before personal agents share information or take action.
fullText:
Instinct, the AI agent now valued at $10 billion as of its latest funding round, is expanding into group chats. The startup announced on Monday that users will be able to add the agent to chats with friends, which could be helpful in certain scenarios like travel planning, snagging event tickets, running fantasy leagues, organizing carpools, or managing who’s bringing what to Thanksgiving.

Notably, the group chats with the AI agent will work even if a user’s friends haven’t joined Instinct, the company said.

With the launch, Instinct moves ahead in its battle with top competitors in the space, like Meta’s Muse. The latter doesn’t yet offer the group chat functionality, though Meta’s older app, Meta AI, can be added to group chats on WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, and Facebook.

Instinct in group chats

Starting today, early access users can add Instinct to group chats. A new Instinct joins and works for the whole group.

Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can… pic.twitter.com/pqJX7ieC7B

— Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) October 5, 2026

Instinct and Muse have been running neck and neck recently, with both of them adding the ability to make phone calls over the past couple of weeks, as their agents try to win more of the consumer AI market. Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Dots, personal AI agents that can also be used in ChatGPT Spaces, collaborative workspaces where the Dots and humans work together.

On X, Instinct founder Noah Shinn explained how Instinct handles users’ privacy and security in group chats. He said a user’s personal Instinct agent will ask permission before connecting with the group’s Instinct agent, and that users can also choose which groups they trust and can remove that trust at any time.

Shinn also said the group’s Instinct is siloed from the users’ personal accounts, which it cannot access. The personal agent will always ask the user’s permission before sharing information or taking any action.

If new members join the group chat, any pending replies from a user’s personal Instinct agent are held before those are shared with the group, too.

“Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can explore options together, agree on a plan and get it done, all in one thread,” Shinn wrote. 

The feature is rolling out initially to Instinct’s early access users but will expand to all users “soon.” To gain access to the new feature (or other recent additions), users can ask their Instinct agent to put them on the list to try it out.

title: TikTok rolls out an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout
snippet: TikTok describes its new Shopping Assistant as a conversational AI agent designed to help users discover and purchase products.
fullText:
TikTok announced Monday that it’s launching an AI shopping assistant and a new in-app checkout feature that lets users buy directly from brands.

TikTok describes its new Shopping Assistant as a conversational AI agent designed to help users discover and purchase products. The company says the assistant understands context and remembers users’ preferences and needs throughout the conversation. It offers real-time, AI-powered shopping guidance, such as product details, shipping information, sizing, availability, and help completing a purchase.

As for the new checkout feature, TikTok says users can buy directly from a brand from their For You feed (the app’s main, algorithm-driven video feed) with one click.

The new features could allow TikTok to capture more of users’ shopping journeys, and potentially more transaction value, without sending them elsewhere. By pairing a shopping assistant with direct payments, TikTok is turning its impulse-driven discovery feed into a place where users can get answers to questions about a product and make a purchase on the spot.

Image Credits:TikTok

By building an AI assistant for shopping directly in its app, TikTok also appears to be hoping that users will stay within its platform when they have questions about a product, rather than turning to outside AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

The company says these new features are being built in partnership with commerce platforms and payment providers including Salesforce, Shopify, Shoplazza, and Stripe, among others.

While TikTok Shop, the app’s in-house marketplace, has been the platform’s main engine for the company’s e-commerce ambitions, these new features broaden its approach beyond the existing shopping hub. Rather than relying on TikTok Shop to drive purchases, the social network is now integrating shopping tools more directly into the broader app, including the For You feed.

The expansion comes as TikTok’s influence on shopping continues to grow. According to TikTok’s Economic Impact Report that was released last week, activity on the platform helped generate $81 billion in GDP for U.S. businesses, while 54 million Americans said they had purchased a product after watching a TikTok video.

TikTok Shop launched in the U.S. in September 2023. The market research firm eMarketer estimates it generated about $15.8 billion in U.S. sales in 2025, representing roughly 18% of all U.S. social commerce.

title: At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI
snippet: Ghost's first product is Core, a personal computer designed specifically for AI agents that can take actions on a person's behalf.
fullText:
For much of his life, Zain Javaid, 19, wanted to be a quant who uses math and data to guide his investment decisions. And for a while, he was one. But he got bored. Then, in 2022, ChatGPT was released, and he told TechCrunch, “I felt fundamentally excited in a way that I never had been before.” 

He became interested in personal AI, and that interest led him to start Ghost, which announced Monday that it has emerged from stealth after a year of building, along with an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Other investors in the round include Abstract, Audacious Ventures, SV Angel, and Nova. His founding team includes Nicholas Chua, 19, Yifei Chen, 24, and Gautam Sharda, 23. 

Ghost’s first product is Core, a personal computer designed specifically for AI agents that can take actions on a person’s behalf. According to Javaid, the idea is to centralize a person’s data, from what’s on their desktop to apps to smart home devices, into one piece of hardware designed to continuously run AI agents that can act as an assistant, perform tasks, and understand a person’s life. “You can run models on existing hardware, but it’s a terrible experience on many levels,” said Javaid, who is also Core’s CEO.

Image Credits:Ghost

Core includes an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 SFF Blackwell GPU (a type of chip commonly used to run AI models), said Javaid, adding that the GPU is bundled into the device’s price, so customers don’t need to buy one separately. He said it also has its own software layer, browser, and filing system and can continuously process information and tasks without constant prompting. Core costs $3,499. Preorders for the first batch open Monday, and shipping is scheduled for the last week of October.

Javaid described Core as a “brain in a box” without a screen, which users access through a phone or app. Voice mode is also available, but users must speak into the Core app rather than the box itself. Core comes with three models preinstalled: Qwen-3.8-Next, Qwen-3.8-27B, and Gemma-4-31B. 

Javaid said users can also install other models from Hugging Face, where developers share AI models, or load their own trained models. Asked how Core differs from a Mac Mini, Apple’s small desktop computer that some people set up to run AI tools, Javaid said Core’s hardware and software were built specifically for running AI agents, with models already installed, while the Mac Mini is a general-purpose computer that can be configured for AI.

“As new models or improvements to existing models come out, we can push out over-the-air updates, similar to how Tesla works,” Javaid said of Core, adding that if a new generation of models comes out, the company asks users whether they want to switch. “Users can also turn on auto-updates so they’re always running the latest generation of a given model.”

The team currently builds the units at its San Francisco facility. Javaid said the goal is to sell a fully functioning computer that doesn’t require complex setup or configuration. He said the models and personal memory run locally, and that all personal information is encrypted so that no cloud provider or third party, including Ghost, can meaningfully access it. He also said users can control how much autonomy they give their Core agents, and that the device is programmed to keep working if Ghost shuts down.

“All of the source code, logic, and model weights live on the device, not the services,” he said. “We build this device to not be dependent on having an outside entity maintaining the service.” 

He said the team is also building a firewall to limit how the agent can use its credentials, such as logins and passwords. The firewall “monitors every outgoing network request on the computer and if it sees the agent performing a sanctioned action or exfiltrating data it shouldn’t, it rejects the request and flags it for user review.”

“The user owns all of it,” he said of the device, memory, and data. “Once you buy the hardware, everything is stored, run, and processed on the device.” 

He said he is not too worried about the competition, including from established tech companies. “People sometimes give incumbents credit for having already built the product because they have the ingredients,” he said. He credited Apple with good hardware and disruption, but said much of what Core is aiming to tackle is software: “The model reasons over your life, how it remembers, how it takes action, how it knows when to reach out,” he continued.

Javaid offered an example of how Core is meant to work: “Core proactively sends you a notification that you might be getting sick because it sees your resting heart rate is elevated, sees from computer history that you were up late working on a project, and has seasonal context that it is flu season in San Francisco.”

The company’s main focus is building a product people love, he said. “If we can’t do that, Apple isn’t the reason we failed,” he said.

Above, Core’s founding team (L-R): Gautam Sharda, 23; Yifei Chen, 24; Zain Javaid, 19; and Nicholas Chua, 19.

title: Meta’s ‘AI Tamagotchi’ Looks to Me Like a Smartwatch Preview for 2027
snippet: As smartwatches head toward becoming AI companions, Meta might be working a new angle.
fullText:
I was in the audience at Meta’s Connect conference in late September when Mark Zuckerberg held up a pendant in his hands and surprise announced the Muse Charm, a little novelty-like device with Meta’s disarmingly adorable Muse AI agent onboard. Muse Charm is coming as soon as December this year.

But the funny thing is, while most people called it an AI Tamagotchi, all I saw was a strapless Apple Watch. Is that what the Muse Charm could be, eventually? A watch as well as a pendant? Is this Meta’s entry to wrist wearables in disguise? I’m still thinking about it…because smartwatches are also on their way to being AI assistants soon, too.

Reports of Meta working on its own watch wearable have been cooking for several years now. At Connect, there were smart glasses galore and even a new glasses-like VR headset coming next year. But things were suspiciously quiet on the wrist wearables front.

			

More from CNET

Meta already has one wrist wearable, the neural band that comes with the Ray-Ban Display glasses. But it received no hardware updates this year, which surprised me. The sensor-studded band uses electromyography, or EMG, to measure skin-contact electrical signals for a set of gesture controls to navigate the heads-up glasses display. Meta’s already ambitiously promised that EMG could open up all sorts of neural input possibilities, even testing the tech in a smart car dashboard prototype.

As far back as last year, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth told me that some sort of display or watch-like evolution of the neural band could be in the works next. And Meta already introduced a partnership with Garmin to link fitness tracking to smart glasses last year.

AI agents as Meta’s new priority

The Muse Charm, however, brings a different piece of the puzzle to the table. Muse AI is Meta’s biggest priority now, clearly, based on its widespread availability on desktops and smartphones and on the company’s intentions to put the new agentic AI on all its smart glasses and, eventually, Meta’s VR Glasses. And where else could Muse work well? Enter the Charm.

The Charm has another watch-like tell. It’s powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite chipset, which already runs on Samsung’s latest smartwatches. The Wear Elite, as I learned from Qualcomm earlier this year, is optimized for a range of AI-ready wearables, ranging from watches to pendants to even glasses. There’s no reason why Meta’s Charm couldn’t easily get a wrist strap…and a watch OS to go with it.

Meta’s neural band doesn’t have a screen yet. Would it ever fuse with Muse Charm?Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Many reasons for a Meta smartwatch

A smartwatch would benefit Meta on several fronts. Clearly, the company wants to keep breaking into lifestyle wearables, and watches could offer another way onto people besides faces. Fitness and health tracking would give Meta data that Muse and its smart glasses could use. And watches are a key part of the glasses interface’s future. Google’s glasses will work with Wear OS watches soon. Apple’s rumored glasses will likely work with Apple Watches.

And Meta has to find a better way to make its neural band more wearable. I find the first-gen neural band fascinating in theory, but an annoying extra thing to charge in practice. If it doesn’t become a watch, or at least a fitness tracker, why wear it at all? The neural band doesn’t even control anything other than Meta’s one line of display glasses right now, but chances are Meta’s going to try to figure out ways it could work with the rest of its smart glasses lineup, and VR too.

Last year I felt like Meta’s neural band felt naked without a watch display (Apple Watch on left, Meta Neural Band on right).Scott Stein/CNET

Google and Apple are already showing how quickly smartwatches are becoming more like AI companions. Gemini lives on Wear OS watches. Apple’s adding memory-assisting audio intelligence modes to its new watches later this fall. Both can tap into Gemini and the new Siri, respectively.

Meta has Muse now. And a charm by the end of the year. Is the watch after that? Meta didn’t have any comment on the topic when I reached out to ask, but I think we’re seeing the beta test in action right in front of our eyes. Or is this the pivot to a modular idea that could be a pendant and a wristworn device, without committing to either? 

One thing’s clear, no matter what: Meta’s looking for ways for that disarmingly adorable Muse mascot to be with us all the time, even without glasses. And the Charm looks like the experiment.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein

title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS privacy controls amid the rise of AI agents
snippet: Amid the rapid rise in AI agents requesting “Full Disk Access” to your Mac, Apple says it is making changes to macOS to protect user privacy. While the company hasn’t shared specifics, Apple says users should understand what it means to give an app such “extraordinary” access to their Mac. more…
fullText:
Amid the rapid rise in AI agents requesting “Full Disk Access” to your Mac, Apple says it is making changes to macOS to protect user privacy.

While the company hasn’t shared specifics, Apple says users should understand what it means to give an app such “extraordinary” access to their Mac.

In a blog post on its Developer website, Apple explains that the Full Disk Access permission in macOS is meant to “allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac.” However, Apple says that “some developers” are using the Full Disk Access setting in macOS in “ways that could put users at risk.”

“We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.”

In response, Apple says it will “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

The company hasn’t shared any additional details about these controls or the changes it plans. Nonetheless, it says that the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents necessitates a greater focus on privacy and security:

“Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”

Apple’s announcement today comes amid the increasing popularity of tools like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. These are always-on AI agents that request substantial access to your personal data, and we’ve already seen some horror stories about Meta Muse in particular.

title: Meta rolling out audio upgrades, turn-by-turn navigation for Ray-Ban smart glasses
snippet: Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. more…
fullText:
Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. 

The most recent system update for Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses is version 129. This update brings two main changes, both to audio playback. Users can now balance audio between the two speakers to best suit their hearing, or set both speakers to mono playback instead of stereo.

Meta explains:

Mono Audio: Hear the same sound on both sides. If you have hearing anomalies, Mono Audio combines the left and right channels so nothing gets missed on the side you can’t hear. Applies to sounds your glasses make, like Meta AI and notifications. Turn it on in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Audio Balance: Shift sound toward your left or right ear, one step at a time, until the balance feels right for your hearing. Applies to sounds your glasses make like Meta AI responses. Adjust it in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Beyond that, update version 128 is broadly available after first debuting earlier in September and it brings some key updates including Spatial Audio support, further anti-tampering tweaks to stop the camera from working if the privacy LED has been mesed with, and also new location features.

	

Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses now feature turn-by-turn walking navigation directions. This pulls your location from your phone and you can also share navigation from your mapping app directly to Meta AI to be used on the glasses.

Pedestrian Navigation: Turn-by-turn pedestrian navigation is here! Get walking directions to your favorite places nearby. Just say “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” For further away places, we’ll send a notification with driving directions to your phone.

Share location from phone to glasses: Open your phone’s mapping app and find a location that you’d like to walk to. Tap Share. Select Meta AI from the list of applications. Navigation will start on your connected glasses.

While the new audio changes are still starting to roll out, the navigation upgrades from version 128 are now broadly available as an update in the Meta AI app.

title: Flai’s AI dealership software is booking 50,000 appointments per month
snippet: Flai's revenue has grown 20x in a year, and the company just closed a $27 million Series A funding round.
fullText:
When Flai was raising its seed round last year, it was just a team of three people pounding the pavement to get car dealerships to use the startup’s software to manage phone calls, emails, and texts. But CEO Ari Polakof was already looking to a more agentic future, where Flai’s AI would handle far more.

One year later, that future has arrived. The startup is working with more than 10 of the top 50 dealer groups in the country, and its AI is being used to answer and engage with customers, run outbound campaigns, and schedule appointments — 50,000 per month — across both sales and service. This has led to a 20x increase in revenue, Polakof told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview.

Flai says this deep integration is helping the startup set itself apart from others trying to get car dealers hooked on AI. The growth is attracting investors, too. On Tuesday, Flai said it had raised a $27 million Series A funding round led by automation-focused firm Base10 Partners. The round included funding from dealers (Friedkin Group and Findlay Automotive), Toyota’s venture arm, Y Combinator, and First Round Capital.

Polakof said Flai’s growth is coming from customers who see the bigger vision of what is essentially an AI-powered customer relationship management software built from the ground up and tailored to the specific need of each dealer.

“Sure, we do answer the phone calls, but we’re following up with customers, we’re alerting the leadership whenever they need to take a look at something, maybe because the customer’s mad, or because you forgot to respond, or promised them something next week,” Polakof said. “We’ve grown quite a bit from just a phone solution to more of a platform. There are plenty of AI companies coming in, but I think that really speaks about the opportunity.” 

Flai claims its software is also flexible. Earlier this year it launched with a luxury dealer in Puerto Rico where customers “switch between Spanish and English mid-conversation,” Flai co-founder Juan Alzugaray wrote in a LinkedIn post. “We started where we always do: inbound service calls. It went well enough that they added sales. And now the group is rolling Flai out across all 8 of their stores,” he wrote.

The result of all this is that dealerships are selling more cars, making more money, and “customers are getting answers faster,” according to one of the groups Flai works with.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, Polakof said much of Flai’s customer growth has come from the dealers talking up the product to their peers.

“If you really do great by them, they also do great by you, and they recommend you, and talk about you,” he said. This has led to Flai generating half of its revenue from new customers, according to Polakof.

Customers are making these referrals because they like Flai’s software, Polakof said, but also because they get up and running quickly. Flai’s software can be live in a dealership 10 days after a contract is signed, and he tells his team — which is now up to around 40 people — that they need to respond to customers within 20 minutes “at most.”

“The common experience, especially around automotive [software] vendors, is — and many are almost traumatized by this — is that they sign the contract and then the company disappears,” he said. “I’m fully focused on making sure that we treat every customer as if they’re our only customer, especially because I know how hard it was to get the first one.”

That speed and customer experience, combined with the knowledge Flai has developed on how dealerships work and what they need, is what Polakof said protects the startup from products like Muse, which Meta has pitched as a one-shot solution for small businesses.

“You get a group of really smart people, and you spend all your days, all your time thinking very deeply about this one space — it’s just so hard to envision that any other platform outside of the space can come in and start going after your customers,” he said.

For all this momentum, there is still one customer Polakof hasn’t been able to land: his own local dealership. 

“I’m actually trying much harder than I should to make them a customer,” he laughed. “I’m sure we will get them by next year.”

title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
snippet: Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data.
fullText:
Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai.

Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday, which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals.

Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active. 

Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers. 

Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling, the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.

Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation.

The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs. This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029. 

Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems. 

Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems. Reflection has already begun testing the concept of a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea.

Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch. 

Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information.

title: Tell Us Which Privacy and Security Apps Are the Most Trustworthy
snippet: Do you use a security software like a VPN or antivirus? Let us and other readers know which one you like the most.
fullText:
When you get security software, it works quietly in the background. So it’s pretty easy to forget about it, until it alerts you that it caught something. CNET’s People’s Picks survey gives you a chance to share what you think about products and services you use daily. We’re keen to learn about how you, our readers, protect your data and devices.”

Whether you’re using a free built-in option or a premium suite, you can help other CNET readers find protection that’s actually worth trusting by sharing your thoughts.

The survey will be open through October and takes only a few minutes to complete. After we gather enough responses. We’ll crunch the numbers and publish a roundup of the winners that CNET readers rated highly.

title: Pinterest’s AI now turns beauty Pins into action plans
snippet: Pinterest’s new AI-powered Beauty Guides translate hair and nail Pins into salon terminology, with estimated costs, appointment times, and maintenance needs.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

7:00 AM PDT · October 6, 2026

Image Credits:Pinterest

		

							

											
									

					

	

Pinterest on Tuesday showed off a new feature that will leverage AI to take action on your saved inspiration from beauty-related Pins, like hair and nail ideas, and turn them into actionable plans you can take with you to the salon. 

“Beauty Guides,” which are powered by the company’s visual intelligence and generative AI technology, Pinterest Intelligence, will translate Pins into terms and phrases used by stylists and nail artists that  everyday users may not know, like “balayage,” “root melt,” or “almond nails.”

The feature is a small but practical way to introduce AI into users’ everyday lives, as it slots into something that people are already doing: bringing a photo of their inspiration to the salon. That’s useful to a large extent, but having the right terminology at hand while you discuss what parts of the look you want to edit or change can be useful as well.

Plus, the guides offer the sort of information that can help users plan for their visit, like the time each part of the process may take and the cost. (Balayage goes into the hundreds of dollars, so that’s information you might like to have up front!)

Image Credits:Pinterest

The action guides will show up when you tap on the “Get the Guide” button within the app, and will then offer details about what, specifically, you should ask for to achieve the same look, the time it takes, price range, and maintenance requirements, like how often you’ll need to trim, tone, or touch up, for instance.

At launch, the feature will work across Pins related to hairstyle, color, nail shape, and finish.

fullText:
Nearly a decade in, foldables have come a long way. Even Apple has noticed all of the fun Android users are having with their bendable smartphones, jumping into the crowd with next month’s iPhone Duo. Unfortunately, you usually need to break an arm and a leg to afford one, but with this one-day-only deal on the last-gen Galaxy Z Fold 7 at Amazon, your entry fee to the foldable club is down to the price of modern slab flagships. You’ll need to hurry though, as this deal is already halfway to selling out.

Amazon is selling Samsung’s excellent 2025 foldable flagship Galaxy Z Fold 7 unlocked for just $1,350 today, reduced even further from the ~$1,500 price point it’s held since its successors launched in mid-summer. This model comes in just a single colorway and storage combination — mint, 256GB — but assuming you aren’t picky, it’s a great price for a foldable that really doesn’t feel all that last-gen in your daily life.

Buy Galaxy Z Fold 7 at Amazon for $1,350

While this year’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra acts as a successor to this model, what’s actually improved on the 2026 release makes for a pretty short list. Sure, the upgrade from the Snapdragon 8 Elite to the 8 Elite Gen 5 is nice to see, and the brighter, anti-reflective main display is hard to argue with. But really, the only big difference between the two is the Fold 8 Ultra’s larger 5,000mAh silicon-carbon battery. You’ll have to settle for a smaller 4,400mAh cell — along with slower 25W charging speeds — though that should be enough to get you through all but your most taxing of days.

Even with a couple of minor sacrifices, considering the way smartphone prices are trending, scoring a foldable for just $50 more than Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra is hard to argue with. Amazon also supports trade-ins, meaning Pixel and Galaxy users can save up to a further $575 on the total price. It might not have that fancy anti-reflective display or a silicon-carbon battery — nor does it have the passport shape seen on the base Fold 8 — but for $1,350, it’s the best deal we’ve seen on a foldable in a while. You’ll have to hurry though, as this deal only goes until the end of today, or until sold out.

title: Looking at Smart Home Deals for Amazon Prime Day? Here Are 4 Picks I Use in My Own Home
snippet: Amazon Prime Days are the time to adopt new smart devices to save time and money. Here’s what I’ve found most useful.
fullText:
Trust me: Smart home devices make awesome home upgrades as well as handy gifts for the person who has everything. But they’re not all created equal. I’ve been testing home devices for years, and I watch for several factors before I recommend them to people, including real-world results for saving money and energy, daily uses that actually make my life easier and features that help protect our privacy.

Here are my favorite devices that pass the test and are available for big discounts during Amazon’s October Prime Day. They include budget items that cost less than dinner and high-end additions, if you want to spend more to get the best. See what your home could use, below.

	

		

	

									

									

						

	

				

			Humidity management could even lead to savings. / Tyler Lacoma/CNET		

	

		

							

											

							The prettiest, most cost-saving home upgrade						

											

							Google Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen)						

									

			

	

			

			

				Get it now			

		

					
			

					

If I had my way, everyone would get a smart thermostat for Christmas. These devices are a major improvement over old heating and cooling controls. They offer eco and vacation modes, easier scheduling through apps, voice controls and algorithms that learn when the house is active or quiet and adjust automatically.

Many smart thermostats pay for themselves within a year or two with energy savings. My Nest model eventually did, and it’s one of the fanciest around, with a dazzling dial display and optional connections to other appliances, too.

				

		
					
			

					It really exists — a thermostat that pays for itself through energy savings while also making heating easier to manage. Plus, it looks great doing it.				

		

	

		

	

									

									

						

	

				

			Nanoleaf has a few unique tricks for easy holiday setups. / Nanoleaf		

	

		

							

											

							Holiday lights done right, and more						

											

							Nanoleaf Smart String Lights, Indoor						

									

			

	

			

			

				Get it now			

		

					
			

If your tired old holiday lights are due for an upgrade, consider these discounted smart lights. Their durable LEDs can display any color you choose through the app, and multiple lengths are available, with the best deal on the extra-long version. The app also lets you set dynamic effects, sync the lights to music or create your own patterns.

With virtually limitless colors and themes, you can use these lights for Halloween, Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year’s and any other color-themed event. That means they can stay up year-round if you really want to get the most out of them.

		
					
			

					Choose every color, pattern and theme with these durable smart lights, making them useful for holidays and year-round events.				

		

	

		

	

									

									

						

	

				

			Zafro's fan has excellent app controls and more. / Zafro		

	

		

							

											

							You won't believe how good cool air feels						

											

							Zafro Smart Tower Fan						

									

			

	

			

			

				Get it now			

		

					
			

					

After testing airflow and more, we can confirm that Zafro’s smart fan is one of the best we’ve ever found, with detailed speed and direction controls, plus up to a 43-foot reach. Do you know how handy it is to control a fan with your voice or a phone app when you’re across the room? It’s very, very nice.

The fan includes timers, modes such as a smart sleep setting so it won’t disturb light sleepers and plenty more choices. You won’t believe how much of a difference this upgrade can make.

				

		
					
			

					This fan did the best in our airflow tests, and has smart features you'll love — especially when things get hot.				

		

What’s the best choice?

My Prime picks can work in all types of homes, depending on what you need. My personal favorite is probably the Nest thermostat because I watched mine pay for itself across a few years of use, but that’s not an upgrade everyone wants to spend money on. Another favorite is the Tapo smart plug pack, because Tapo is one of the very few smart plug makers that offer energy monitoring, which is also nice for saving energy when you’re using something like a space heater or my Zafro tower fan pick.

			

More from CNET

Should I wait until Prime Day?

The best parts of these smart home deals are likely to kick in on Prime Day, so I’d say it’s worth waiting a day or two to see how much you can save. Just keep this list bookmarked so you remember what models to get.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.

title: ChatGPT is adding new ads
snippet: OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month. more…
fullText:
OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month.

Announced today, OpenAI will be adding a “new visual ad format” to the ChatGPT app that shows when prompts are processing. Specifically, these will start showing during image generation.

OpenAI explains:

Our new visual ad format helps people imagine how products and services could fit into their lives. Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy. For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.

Initially, we’ll test this new ad format during image generation in ChatGPT. Ads will be clearly labeled, and remain separate from the image being created. As with our other ad formats, advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Previously, OpenAI tested ads that would show up at the bottom of answers with advertisements related to that prompt. An example showed a grocery delivery ad below a recipe response.

	

As for when you might start seeing these new ads in ChatGPT, OpenAI says it will be testing the format in its app for users in the US starting “later this month,” but a broad rollout isn’t confirmed yet.

OpenAI’s post touts that early findings with its ChatGPT ads have found lower cost per acquisition rates and that businesses are finding higher rates of new customers via the ads.

title: The first thing you should do on Googlebook is fix the trackpad
snippet: If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box. more…
fullText:
If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box.

Every Googlebook in this initial wave comes with a haptic trackpad, but they also seem to have a slight headache out of the box.

The cursor is incredibly slow.

“Touchpad accleration” on Googlebook, at least by default, is considerably slower than other platforms such as Windows and macOS. It’s something that we’ve all noticed here on the 9to5Google team as we’ve started using Googlebook machines this week across multiple models. It’s far from unusable, but it’s very jarring compared to any other laptop you might go buy at the store today. 

	

Luckily, it can be fixed fairly easily. Go to Settings > Device & accessories > Touchpad > Cursor speed  and you’ll be able to adjust the setting to your preferences. For me, that meant maxing it out to get something more akin to my other machines. 

You’ll have to complete inital setup before you can adjust this setting.

title: GrayKey maker can reportedly bypass the iPhone’s ‘Inactivity Reboot’ security feature
snippet: As reported by 404 Media, Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass the iPhone security feature that automatically reboots devices if they haven’t been unlocked for 72 hours. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As reported by 404 Media, Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass the iPhone security feature that automatically reboots devices if they haven’t been unlocked for 72 hours. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Nearly two years ago, the iOS 18.1 update introduced Inactivity Reboot, a feature that forces iPhone reboots in case they haven’t been unlocked for 72 hours.

In essence, this feature makes it harder for law enforcement and forensic tools to access data on a locked iPhone, since a reboot causes the device to return to a Before First Unlock (BFU) state, rather than remaining in the less restrictive After First Unlock (AFU) state.

When an iPhone is in BFU, certain sensitive data remains protected by encryption keys that only become available after the user enters their passcode for the first time, thus putting the device in AFU.

From that point on, more of the device’s data remains accessible until the iPhone is rebooted again, which returns it to BFU.

Automatically rebooting an iPhone means that even if a device is seized by law enforcement, it can return to BFU before investigators can access it, since obtaining a warrant or transporting the device to a forensic lab can take time.

As 404 Media noted when iOS 18.1 was released, the feature can also make it harder for thieves or other bad actors to keep a stolen iPhone in AFU long enough to develop or use a way to break into it.

GrayKey reportedly gets around Inactivity Reboot

404 Media reported today that, based on an “educational and tutorial video, which was made exclusively for law enforcement agents and appears to be dated early 2025,” Magnet Forensics, the company behind the GrayKey phone unlocking tool, appears to have developed a way to bypass the iPhone’s Inactivity Reboot feature.

According to the report, Magnet developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve, as well as an Evidence Preservation Mode for its existing GrayKey hardware.

Both are reportedly designed to maintain an iPhone’s forensic state without immediately exposing the data stored on the device, allowing law enforcement to keep that state intact while waiting for authorization to search it.

The report notes that while the video doesn’t detail the technical mechanism behind the workaround, it explains that GrayKey can preserve an iPhone’s AFU state even if the device reboots.

From the report:

“That AFU state is captured,” by GrayKey Preserve and Evidence Preservation Mode, the employee says. “Even if that device does reboot for any number of reasons, memory maintenance or the power is lost or whatever, the AFU state is not lost. This is the true magic behind the GrayKey Preserve and the Evidence Preservation Mode function.”

404 Media reached out to Apple and Magnet Forensics, but neither responded to a request for comment. They also consulted iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen, who said Magnet may have found a way to manipulate the iPhone’s clock, or to turn off the processes responsible for expiring certain data altogether.

While the video appears to date from early 2025, it is unclear how long the technology has been available to law enforcement, whether it has been used in actual investigations, or whether the workaround remains effective against the latest versions of iOS.

title: Full Disk Access on Mac: Here’s what Apple must, and must not, do
snippet: We’ve seen a number of examples of why giving Meta’s Muse app full disk access to your Mac is a very bad idea, and yet another major privacy issue has recently been discovered. It’s now been found that Muse analyzes your communication with everyone in your life on an hourly basis. Apple is rightly concerned about the development, and in a blog post says that it will be introducing additional controls around the Full Disk Access feature that’s been enabling the problems … more…
fullText:
We’ve seen a number of examples of why giving Meta’s Muse app full disk access to your Mac is a very bad idea, and yet another major privacy issue has recently been discovered. It’s now been found that Muse analyzes your communication with everyone in your life on an hourly basis.

Apple is rightly concerned about the development, and in a blog post says that it will be introducing additional controls around the Full Disk Access feature that’s been enabling the problems … 

Meta recently launched its Muse Personal AI Agent for iPhone and Mac. Despite the obvious inadvisability of giving a Meta app unfettered access to everything on your Apple devices, the app quickly jumped to the top of the App Store.

Predictably, it wasn’t long before things started to go horribly wrong. Things haven’t gotten any better since then, with Wired reporting that security researcher Karan Joshi found Meta had instructed Muse to extract all of the information needed to construct a complete map of all of your relationships.

One of Muse’s instructions appears to be the ability for it to create “a page for every person in the user’s life.” This hourly process involves compiling data on family, partners, friends, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow,” the instructions say […]

“Where they live, what they do, the threads that recur (the apartment move, the shared savings goal),” the instructions say. They add, too, that the model could record the “dates that matter,” such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person’s history could include backstory like “the trip in March, the argument that got resolved, the milestone last week.”

Apple tightening use of Full Disk Access

You would think a permission prompt to give an app “full disk access” to your Mac would be self-explanatory, but it appears not. Even tech-savvy people have been granting this access-all-areas pass to their machines without appreciating just how dangerous a step it is.

Apple says the feature was intended for backup apps, but developers are now using it for many more things, including AI agents. The company has said it intends to “introduce additional controls” to ensure users fully understand what they are doing if they grant this permission.

Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.

Here’s what Apple must – and must not – do

Apple says it is “critical” to take this step, and I fully agree. When it’s become clear that the existing permission request doesn’t fully communicate the gravity of granting it, it’s essential that Apple ensure users genuinely understand what it is they are allowing.

What I’d like to see is far more explicit text advising people against doing it unless they are certain they understand the consequences. Something along the lines:

This app is requesting full disk access to your Mac, aka an access-all-areas pass to your data. Apple intended this feature to be used only by backup apps. If you grant permission, this app will be able to read all of your personal data, including all of your messages with other people. Giving permission is extremely dangerous and should never be done unless you are completely confident that you understand what the app will do with your data and that you have complete trust in the developer. Your default response to this permission request should be No.

Essentially, there is no wording that would be too strong. I’d also be fine with a one-off confirmation of the apps already given this permission.

	

However, what Apple absolutely must not do is to make the mistake it made with macOS Sequoia over screen recording. Sure, this is also incredibly dangerous and very strong warnings are appropriate, but what Apple did then was to force us all to confirm these permissions on a weekly basis, as well as after every restart. 

This was widely condemned as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing “a subscription you didn’t buy and can’t cancel.” In my view, Apple already goes too far in this direction with its occasional requests for repeated permission confirmations on iPhone. I gave Citymapper permission to access my location so that it can continue to provide directions in the background, for example, and no, Apple, I really don’t need you to check I still want this.

Yes, issue the strongest of warnings against granting full disk access, but if someone chooses to do so, then macOS must accept their decision. No forced confirmations, weekly or otherwise, thank you.

fullText:
Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

MacPaw spent nearly two decades building consumer software for Mac users. CleanMyMac is one of the Mac utilities on the market, and it’s my go-to when I need to free up hard drive space, uninstall apps, etc. The company is making a different kind of bet with Leebry, a Work AI platform aimed at helping IT teams.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The AI trust numbers

MacPaw’s 2026 AI at Work report is where you see the issue IT faces, as they found that 90% of companies deploy AI without thoroughly auditing their internal knowledge base first. That means that internal AI tools are answering employee questions based on whatever it can find, including old product docs, outdated policies, and random Reddit discussion forums.

In this survey, MacPaw found that 6 in 10 IT leaders see a real disconnect between what their C-Suite expects from AI tools (thanks to LinkedIn feeds) and what their teams can safely and accurately deliver. That gap is where most AI disappointment lives, and it’s the problem Leebry is attempting to solve for IT teams.

What Leebry actually does

Leebry began as an internal MacPaw hackathon project in 2025. The problem it was solving was employees repeatedly asking the same questions internally, even when the answers already existed somewhere in the company’s documentation, intranets, Slack threads, etc. MacPaw built a Slack bot to surface those answers and point employees to the exact source. Within a few months, it was resolving 30% of MacPaw’s own level 1 IT tickets, so that became the foundation for what they’re launching today with Leebry.

The platform automates level 1 support tickets, handles access provisioning and removal as employees join, move roles, or leave, and answers employee questions across the tools they already use. Every Leebry response links back to its source, so employees can verify the answer rather than just trust it (and prove it), and can flag stale or outdated information that could affect accuracy. That last part is the direct product response to the 90% knowledge audit problem from their own research.

One detail worth calling out for security-conscious IT folks: Leebry is permission-aware, meaning it authenticates each user and surfaces only the information they are permitted to see. That matters more than it sounds as a lot of AI tools draw on a shared knowledge pool and let users surface things they shouldn’t access. Leebry also ships with an MCP server that exposes the device management control plane to AI agents, with admin-set guardrails on every action, so teams can delegate repetitive work to agents without giving up control over what those agents can actually do.

For IT orgs that work extensively with Apple, the access provisioning aspect is interesting. Automating access changes as people move within the organization can be a huge pain point for SMBs without a dedicated IAM team. Most of the time, it’s manual, it’s slow, and departing employees end up with access that should have been revoked days earlier. I’ve run into this myself quite a bit.

“Businesses don’t need another tool to check, they need work taken off their plate, without sacrificing oversight or control,” said Dan Jaenicke, Director of B2B Product Development at MacPaw.

Wrap up

The fair question here is why an IT team should trust a consumer Mac software company to build enterprise tooling. I think the answer is actually in the product’s origin story. MacPaw built Leebry to solve their own internal IT problem first, which is a better foundation than most enterprise software gets. It wasn’t built to make money. It was built to solve a customer (even internal) problem, so it’ll work well for other teams. The reality is all orgs have docs spread out across team chat, file sharing, intranets, etc and we’re all guilty of asking for someone else to find it for us.

Leebry aims to make it easy for IT to solve the same questions folks ask over and over again.

title: Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599
snippet: Google has quietly raised the price of its mid-range Pixel 10a by $100, giving the device a starting price of $599. more…
fullText:
Google has quietly raised the price of its mid-range Pixel 10a by $100, giving the device a starting price of $599.

Effective as of today at the Google Store, Pixel 10a has jumped from $499 to $599. The reason is obvious, of course, with the current skyrocketing costs of components such as memory. Google has not officially commented on the price hike yet, though.

This follows Google issuing a price increase to each of its new Pixel 11 devices compared to the prior generation. 

When Google confirmed the Pixel 11 would be more expensive, the company said that this would eventually impact “in-market Pixel phones” which, at the time, we speculated could include Pixel 10a.

	

The 128GB base Pixel 10a is $599 as of today, with the 256GB model at $699. The updated prices have already kicked in at Amazon and Best Buy, and Google Store now shows Pixel 10a at $849 in Canada, £599 in the UK, and €649 in Europe.

	

In our review of Pixel 10a, we called the device a “well-rounded experience” for its $499 price, but a $100 jump certainly makes that a tougher conversation, especially considering Google’s mid-ranger is at this point using a two-generation-old chipset in its Tensor G4. But, of course, Google is far from alone here. Just this week, Samsung also issued price hikes across the Galaxy lineup including flagship and mid-range devices alike.

title: The Pixel 3a might be the most important Google smartphone to date
snippet: Google Pixel was designed to be a premium smartphone effort, but that all changed in 2019 with the debut of the Pixel 3a. The budget-conscious launch went on to be a turning point for the Pixel’s history and, looking back, it might just be the single most important Google smartphone ever. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel was designed to be a premium smartphone effort, but that all changed in 2019 with the debut of the Pixel 3a. The budget-conscious launch went on to be a turning point for the Pixel’s history and, looking back, it might just be the single most important Google smartphone ever.

Looking back over the past decade of Pixel smartphones, I’m not sure you can point at any one device and say it was more important than the Pixel 3a. The original Pixel set the foundation, of course, and Pixel 6 launched Google’s efforts into a new era, but Pixel 3a gave Google a taste of what it was always after – market success.

The Pixel 3a almost immediately shot up to the top of best-seller lists, massively propelled Google’s US smartphone sales, and was the driving force behind setting Google’s first big shipment records. That success ultimately led to several Pixel A-series successors that have similarly resonated in the market. These more affordable devices just nail the fundamentals at a price that’s hard to beat, especially considering the cost of a Pixel 10a is only $100 more (annnnnnd now it’s $200) than the Pixel 3a originally started at.

Google is finding at least some success in the flagship market nowadays. Pixel phones are very much hitting their stride in 2026 not only in terms of design and functionality, but also in the market as a whole. I’d very much argue, though, that the Pixel 3a was the lifejacket that kept this project going. The failure of the Pixel 4 left scars on Google’s smartphone efforts, but the Pixel 3a’s resounding success was surely a huge deciding factor on what would come next.

	
	

And, in 2026, I think this phone holds up remarkably well from a hardware perspective. There are modern budget phones that cost just as much as the Pixel 3a did when it came out that feel a lot worse than this one. The Pixel 3a is long dead at this point with software support having ended in 2022, but its legacy lives on.

Did you ever own a Pixel 3a?

title: OpenAI launches Dots, new ‘always-on agents’ you can assign tasks to
snippet: Right as Meta’s Muse avatar agent has taken the AI world by storm, OpenAI is today announcing Dots as “always-on agents” you can customize to your needs. more…
fullText:
Right as Meta’s Muse avatar agent has taken the AI world by storm, OpenAI is today announcing Dots as “always-on agents” you can customize to your needs.

Out of OpenAI DevDay 2026, Dots are OpenAI’s answer to giving users a way to assign tasks to an AI agent to run in the background. The company says that Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, has “their own cloud computer” and can use that to accomplish tasks that you have assigned. You can interact with Dots via ChatGPT, Slack, or Teams once they’ve been set up.

OpenAI explains:

Dots are frontier intelligence that have your back. Powered by GPT‑6 Astra, they have their own cloud computer, learn from feedback over time, and can work towards your goals 24/7. Through our ecosystem of plugins, they can readily connect to over 4,000 apps, giving them the tools to help wherever you need them.

Your dot is always within reach, whether it is through ChatGPT, Slack, or Teams. You can ask questions, explore ideas, and give feedback along the way; or you can simply hop on a voice call when you need to talk something out. The more you work together, the more your dot learns your preferences, how you think, and what good looks like to you.

Some examples of how OpenAI says it is using Dots internally include having Dots automatically investigate bugs when they are mentioned in Slack, creating working apps when a “new design” is ready, and more. Another example saw a Dot notice on its own that an invoice had not been sent, to which it created that invoice for the user’s approval. Dots do “proactive research” when not actively working on a task through read-only connections with tools you’ve connected.

	

As the user, you can see a Dot’s cloud computer at any time while it is working on a task, as well as giving it permission to use your computer. 

OpenAI further adds that Dots follow the same permissions and controls as ChatGPT, and they also support custom rules around when they can act on their own or require approval from you. 

Dots are available today to Pro and Business Premium users, with Enterprise users also able to try it out when workspace admins approve it. One Dot is included with these plans, with OpenAI saying you’ll be able to add more in the future. Dots must be created via the ChatGPT desktop app or browser, but can be interacted with via the mobile app after that.

title: If Apple’s AI suggestions in Messages annoys you, there’s a solution coming
snippet: The current beta of iOS 27.2 includes a Siri AI “suggested actions” feature in the Messages app that some will consider useful and others find annoying. A developer who has found a number of unannounced features has discovered that Apple is seeking to keep everyone happy with a new set of options … more…
fullText:
The current beta of iOS 27.2 includes a Siri AI “suggested actions” feature in the Messages app that some will consider useful and others find annoying. 

A developer who has found a number of unannounced features has discovered that Apple is seeking to keep everyone happy with a new set of options …

Suggested Actions in Messages

Suggested Actions were present in the initial iOS 27 beta, but Apple later pulled the feature after complaints that some of the suggestions were rather random. It subsequently returned in the beta of iOS 27.2. Here’s how Apple describes it:

Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of users’ conversations, making it easier than ever to get things done, such as creating a reminder or a note. For example, if someone asks for photos, Messages can also help users find the right ones, recognizing keywords, locations, and people in their library to find the best options.

In the first example shown above, a group message chat contains a request for some shopping and to bring something left behind. The Messages app offers one-tap options to Add to Reminders and Add to Notes. In the second example, someone asks for specific photos to be shared, and the Messages app offers a button which leads directly to a search for matching photos.

Two ways to hide unwanted suggestions

Leaker pdfu found new controls in iOS 27.2 beta 3 to selectively toggle off unwanted suggestions.

These allow suggestions to be toggled off by category, or you can let Siri AI monitor which ones you do and don’t use, and have it automatically hide the categories you haven’t used in the last 30 days.

These options aren’t yet live in the beta, but we can likely expect to see them soon.

9to5Mac’s Take

I’m certainly one of those who found many of them more annoying than useful, while I know others who are big fans, so this change ought to keep everyone happy.

title: OpenAI details new text watermarking system for ChatGPT, Codex, and the API
snippet: OpenAI today announced how it will comply with the EU AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to mark AI-generated text in a way that makes it identifiable. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
OpenAI today announced how it will comply with the EU AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to mark AI-generated text in a way that makes it identifiable. Here are the details.

A bit of context

A few months ago, Anthropic sparked controversy when it announced that, to comply with the EU AI Act, Claude would start watermarking text by slightly adjusting its word choice.

In a nutshell, every so often, Claude chooses between words that would work equally well based on a hidden pattern, which Anthropic says has no practical impact on the meaning, quality, or readability of its responses.

Anthropic also developed a detector that can look for that pattern in a piece of text, and can tell whether it likely came from Claude.

The detector can’t be used to determine whether text came from OpenAI or any other competitor, since Claude’s watermark is generated using a secret key specific to Anthropic’s system.

At the height of the controversy, Anthropic stressed that Claude would not be alone, noting that several other major AI providers were also implementing marking systems to comply with the EU’s requirements.

Today, OpenAI announced its own solution, which relies on a similar approach, albeit with a much more limited rollout and scope.

OpenAI’s text watermarking system

According to OpenAI, “API customers globally will be able to opt in to text watermarking for select models” starting today, while the company “will add an invisible watermark to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union” in the coming weeks.

This means that in the API, text watermarking will remain off by default for now, while in ChatGPT and Codex, it will initially be limited to eligible users only in the European Union.

OpenAI also opened applications for access to its text watermark detector, which will initially be limited to approved researchers and expert organizations as the company works to evaluate and improve the technology.

And speaking of accuracy, OpenAI is very clear that the detection technology still has significant limitations, as it can produce both false negatives and false positives, particularly with shorter texts or content in specific domains, “such as mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice.”

Here’s OpenAI on textGrain, which is its text watermarking technology:

Our text watermarking technology, textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark. More details about how textGrain works can be found in our technical report⁠, which will be updated with additional details in the coming weeks. We also plan to make the technology available in open source so that others can build on it.

The company also noted that, in addition to being harder to detect in shorter passages, the watermark can be significantly weakened by editing:

In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%. Replacing 25% of words reduced it to 17%.

Interestingly, OpenAI’s comparison of watermarked and unwatermarked text showed that watermarked outputs actually scored slightly higher on several benchmarks, despite the company saying it found no meaningful difference in overall performance.

title: Glimpse wants to give hardware companies an X-ray view of every critical part
snippet: Called Explore, Glimpse's new image processing software lets hardware makers speed up quality control checks using CT scanners.
fullText:
Recalls are no joke. Take the one that sidelined every Chevy Bolt made between 2017 and 2022: A problem at an LG battery factory caused some parts inside the cells to be installed improperly, which ultimately cost LG $1.9 billion.

Pretty much every major manufacturer has to deal with recalls. In the EV space alone, Volkswagen, Stellantis, Hyundai, Toyota, and others have all suffered through them. 

“The majority of those major quality issues could have been caught with CT scanning. And the reason why they weren’t is because it’s way too slow to do any kind of statistical sampling,” Eric Moch, co-founder and CEO of Glimpse, told TechCrunch.

To help companies find more defects, Glimpse has developed a way for battery manufacturers to inspect cells 10 to 30 times faster by significantly boosting throughput on their existing CT scanners. Using Glimpse’s software, manufacturers could scan tens of thousands of cells per day, up from the current handful, Moch said. A customer “super scanner” that Glimpse is developing with partners could complete a scan in a second or two, he added.

Batteries aren’t the only parts to suffer from costly defects, of course, so Glimpse is launching a new product, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. Called Explore, the product will let customers in industries such as aerospace, automotive, electronics, and medical devices use the startup’s image processing software to speed up quality control checks using CT scanners in their labs and development environments.

Glimpse currently has over 100 customers, such as Anker, Lucid, and the U.S. Navy, and currently generates revenue in the “mid seven-figure” range, Moch said. Customers include both buyers and sellers of batteries.

To wring more speed out of traditionally slow CT scanners, the startup has written its own image processing pipeline, which compresses scans and cleans them up. It’s built around deep learning algorithms, and much of the initial processing happens on edge computers deployed at a customer’s site. “It does all of the heavy lifting before sending the output to the cloud,” Moch said.

Altogether, the combination of quality improvements and compression make for clear images that load within seconds in a web browser, the company claims. “You don’t have to wait minutes or even sometimes hours for that data to load,” he said. 

Alongside scanned images, Glimpse’s dashboard will also show customers part measurements they specify. In the case of batteries, it might measure the distance between layers in a battery cell. If they start deviating from the norm, Glimpse’s software will flag it and highlight it in the scanned images. “They can see with their own eyes the defects that they care about,” Moch said. The deep learning algorithms also take into account customer input, retraining themselves along the way.

Customers who don’t have their own CT scanners can ship parts to Glimpse, which will use its own CT scanner in the Boston area. The company said it is opening a second Scan On Demand center in the San Francisco Bay Area.

“We expect this scanning service to actually be a bigger market. You can spend a couple hundred bucks or a few thousand dollars on Glimpse, and you don’t have to buy a very expensive piece of equipment,” Moch said. “And one day, when it makes sense for you, you buy the scanner and then you run our software on top of it.”
